source.title: On the Double Descent of Random Features Models Trained with SGD
source.authors: Fanghui Liu; J. Suykens; V. Cevher

page_placements.theme: Capacity, sample size and optimization or stopping times

record.tranche_reason: The study tests double descent with random-features regression trained by averaged SGD, a different model and optimization setup from deep-network size sweeps.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-MSE sweeps over random-feature count and a theoretical variance bound relevant to double descent. The plotted MSE values are not numerically stated in the text. It also compares generalization at 50 and 100 epochs, but does not report an epoch-wise fall-rise-fall curve. Findings cited from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study derives non-asymptotic bias and variance bounds for random-features regression trained by averaged SGD. It also plots test MSE against m/n on MNIST and synthetic data. These results bear on whether risk falls again past the interpolation threshold in a non-deep model class (V4), and on whether variance carries the peak (V6). Random features are a fixed-first-layer two-layer model, not a deep-network size sweep, so V1 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that averaged-SGD random-features regression recovers double descent, with a monotonically decreasing bias bound and a unimodal variance bound. They add that constant step-size SGD loses no convergence rate relative to the min-norm solution, while polynomial-decay step-size slows the rate. They flag two limitations: random features are far from practical networks, and only single-pass SGD is analysed.
record.recipe_differences: Uses random features with fixed Gaussian-initialized first-layer weights and averaged, single-pass SGD on the output layer; evaluates random-feature ratios on MNIST and a synthetic regression dataset rather than sweeping practical deep-network sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different step-size settings in additional experiments and compares 50 versus 100 epochs on a synthetic dataset; it says the additional step-size experiments retain decreasing bias and unimodal variance.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic data, averaged SGD run for 100 epochs generalizes better than at 50 epochs, though still slightly worse than the min-norm solution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In random-features regression, more SGD epochs move the solution toward min-norm generalization performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Constant-step averaged SGD matches the min-norm/ridge convergence rate (O(1/√n) excess risk with m=O(√n)).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SGD training of random-features models incurs no rate loss versus the closed-form interpolator.

record.code_released: Supplemental material is stated to include code, data, and instructions; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The empirical test-MSE and component curves are presented as plots without numerical values in the text. Experiments are limited to random-features regression and single-pass SGD; the authors identify the distance from practical neural networks as a limitation.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results left out.

untested.parts: No sweep of deep-network size; the random-features model fixes the first layer.
No test-error curve over training time; SGD is single-pass, with only a 50 vs 100 epoch comparison.
No result showing that more samples raise test error near the threshold.
Only the random-features model class is tested; no classical U-shaped regime and no other model classes.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Label-noise level is not varied (τ² appears only as a constant). No multiple or triple peaks. No test of optimally tuned regularization removing the peak.

missing.what: Synthetic regression test-MSE curve: a phase transition at 2m=n for both min-norm and averaged SGD under constant initialization (n from 10 to 400, d=50)
Bias bound and empirical bias components (B1–B3) decrease monotonically in m/n, showing the peak is not bias-driven
Different step-sizes preserve monotone bias and unimodal variance (V3 peak)

record.verdict_notes: R1 and R2 values are figure-only, so exact MSE values are not available. I dropped the reader's V6 limits_scope label on R4/R5. Variance components that rise and then plateau, while the interaction component V3 peaks, refine where the variance peak sits rather than showing a condition where V6 fails. Noise dependence is implied only by the τ² scaling of the bound; it is never varied experimentally. On MNIST the label noise is assumed to be N(0,1) in order to compute the components.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not sweep the size of deep networks; its random-features model fixes the first-layer weights and optimizes the output layer.
No test-error curve over training epochs is reported; the paper compares only 50 and 100 epochs in one experiment.
Although the synthetic experiment uses training-set sizes ranging from n=10 to n=400, the text does not report that increasing sample size near the interpolation threshold raises test error.
Tests random-features regression, not a broad sweep across model classes or the full classical U-shaped regime.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.

The study examines bias and variance behavior, but does not vary label-noise level to test what drives the peak, test multiple or triple peaks, or test whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The study does not re-count complexity using an effective number of parameters.

rows.subject: RF regression trained with averaged SGD
rows.operation_detail: Derived an upper bound for variance across the under- and over-parameterized regimes.
rows.measure: Upper bound on variance contribution to averaged excess risk
rows.value: γ0²rτ² mn^(ζ−1) if m≤n; γ0²rτ²(1+n^(ζ−1)+n/m) if m>n; authors describe the bound as unimodal in m
rows.note: This is a theoretical bound, not a numerical measurement of the label-noise effect.
rows.check: This is an upper bound, not an exact risk. The authors note the bounds come via a Minkowski inequality and are not lower bounds (App. A.2). Unimodality of a bound is suggestive, not exact. Its noise dependence enters only through τ², which is never varied.

source_check.correct: Theorem 2 gives Variance ≲ γ₀ r0 τ² times mn^(ζ−1) for m≤n, and times (1+n^(ζ−1)+n/m) for m>n; r0 denotes the Assumption 4 constant in the extracted text. The prefactor contains γ₀, not γ₀². State: cannot_determine for an actual variance-driven risk peak from this upper bound alone.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3, Theorem 2 and remark (i), lines 468–482; Appendix G.4, lines 5888–5912; Appendix A.2, lines 1231–1237.
source_check.problem: The prefactor is transcribed incorrectly, and an upper bound's unimodality alone does not establish the actual effect.

rows.check: Variance component V1 rises for 2m<n and then stays flat; it does not peak. This shows the peak sits in one variance component (V3), not that variance fails to drive the peak. It refines the decomposition rather than qualifying V6.

relationships.condition: Random-features regression (Gaussian kernel) on MNIST 3 vs 7 with n=600, using averaged SGD (ζ=0.5) and the min-norm solution
relationships.reason: Both solvers show test MSE peaking at 2m=n and falling again past it (R1, R2). The text adds the same pattern on synthetic data (Fig. 3a), which no row records.
relationships.display_finding: Both solvers showed test MSE peaking at 2m=n and falling beyond it, with the same pattern also reported on synthetic data.
